oneSentence: A planned process for strengthening people, organisations and systems so they can carry out tasks well, sustainably and with less outside help.
plainExplanation:
Capacity-building means helping people and institutions develop the skills, tools, processes and resources needed to do a job well. In AI governance and public administration, that can include training staff, improving data practices, setting clear roles, creating guidance and building technical infrastructure.

What goes in can include money, time, trainers, policy advice, software, equipment and partnerships. But those inputs alone are not the goal. The process matters: people learn, organisations change how they work, and systems are set up so the work can continue after a workshop or project ends.

What happens during capacity-building often includes assessing gaps, choosing priorities, designing support, practising new tasks and checking what improved. For example, a ministry might train officials to assess AI risks, create a review checklist and assign a team to maintain it. That is broader than one training session.

What comes out should be stronger ability to act: staff who can do the work, organisations that have procedures, and institutions that can keep improving over time. It is often confused with aid, equipment donations or awareness-raising, but those are only parts of the picture unless they lead to lasting capability.

everydayAnalogy.title: Preparing a school team to run a science fair every year
everydayAnalogy.story: A school wants to hold a science fair, but only one teacher has done it before. Instead of asking that teacher to manage everything again, the school creates a planning guide, trains several teachers, gives student volunteers clear roles and stores reusable signs and forms in one shared cupboard. The first fair takes effort, but by the next year the team can run it with much less outside help. The result is not just one event; it is the ability to repeat the event reliably.

everydayAnalogy.limitation: The analogy is simpler than real capacity-building. In governments and international organisations, the work may involve laws, budgets, procurement, digital systems, language needs and coordination across many institutions. Also, real capacity-building is not only about repeating one known task; it can include learning how to assess new technologies and manage risks as circumstances change.

visual.title: How capacity-building turns support into lasting capability
visual.learningObjective: Show that capacity-building is a sequence from identifying gaps to sustaining improved performance, not just a one-off training event.
visual.description: A left-to-right step diagram with five connected boxes. Read from gap identification to sustained capability. Each box names one stage and a short note explains how inputs are turned into lasting organisational ability.

steps.label: 1. Find the gap
steps.explanation: Identify what people or institutions cannot yet do well, and why.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw a box labelled 'Find the gap' with small icons for skills, tools and rules; add a note below: 'What is missing?'.

steps.label: 2. Plan support
steps.explanation: Choose the mix of training, guidance, tools, staffing or partnerships needed.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw a second box labelled 'Plan support' connected by an arrow; show a checklist icon with five short lines.

steps.label: 3. Build and practise
steps.explanation: Deliver training, create procedures and let people use them in real tasks.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw a third box labelled 'Build and practise'; include icons for a workshop, a document and a computer.

steps.label: 4. Embed in routine work
steps.explanation: Assign roles, budgets and review processes so the new ability stays in place.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw a fourth box labelled 'Embed in routine work'; add icons for an organisational chart and calendar.

steps.label: 5. Improve over time
steps.explanation: Measure results and update the approach as needs change.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw a fifth box labelled 'Improve over time'; add a loop arrow and a simple chart icon.

visual.interaction: On hover or tap, each step reveals one example: training staff, drafting guidance, buying needed tools, assigning responsibility, or reviewing results.
visual.accessibilityDescription: The diagram shows five stages in order. First, an organisation identifies a gap in skills, tools or rules. Second, it plans the support needed, such as training, guidance, equipment or partnerships. Third, people build skills and practise using new procedures in real work. Fourth, the organisation embeds the new way of working through assigned roles, budgets and regular review. Fifth, it measures what changed and updates the approach. The main message is that capacity-building is a process that creates lasting capability, not a single event.
visual.reducedMotionDescription: A static five-box step diagram appears in one view, with arrows between the stages and the same example text shown under each box instead of hover effects.

workedExample.scenario: A national digital agency wants staff to review simple AI procurement proposals instead of relying entirely on external consultants.
workedExample.input: Starting point: 12 staff members, only 2 have prior experience; budget for six months; one draft procurement checklist.
process: The agency surveys staff and finds three main gaps: understanding AI risks, using a common review checklist and documenting decisions.
It runs four half-day training sessions, improves the checklist into a two-page template and appoints 3 focal points to answer routine questions.
Staff practise on 10 sample proposals; after feedback, the template is revised to add sections on data quality, human oversight and vendor claims.
By month six, 9 of the 12 staff can complete a first review themselves, while complex cases still go to specialists.
workedExample.result: The output is not just trained staff. The agency now has a reusable process, named focal points and a standard template, so ordinary reviews can be handled internally and more consistently.

unWorkplaceExample.scenario: A UN country team is reviewing programme monitoring data and wants staff to use approved analytical tools more confidently and consistently. Capacity-building could include training on data quality checks, guidance on responsible use, clear approval steps and a small support group for questions.
unWorkplaceExample.relevance: This helps teams analyse information more reliably, reduces uneven practice between offices and supports better oversight of programme decisions.
unWorkplaceExample.caution: Do not place personal, confidential or protection-sensitive monitoring data into an unapproved public AI service. Use approved systems, follow data protection rules and keep human review in the loop.

whyItMatters: If you hear a proposal about AI, digital government or public services, capacity-building tells you whether people and institutions will actually be able to use the new rules or tools responsibly. A policy can look strong on paper and still fail if staff lack training, if procedures are unclear or if no one is assigned to maintain the system. Asking about capacity-building helps non-specialists check whether a plan is realistic, fair across countries and likely to last beyond a pilot project or outside consultant.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Capacity-building just means giving people a workshop.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Training can help, but lasting capability usually also needs procedures, tools, roles, resources and follow-up. A workshop without changes in routine work often fades quickly.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: It only matters for countries with fewer resources.
commonMisconceptions.correction: All organisations need it when technology, rules or risks change. A well-resourced institution can still lack the skills, coordination or processes needed to use AI responsibly.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Buying software or equipment counts as capacity-building by itself.
commonMisconceptions.correction: New tools may support capacity-building, but they do not create capability on their own. People must know when and how to use them, and the organisation needs governance around them.

simpleVsTechnical.simple: In plain terms, capacity-building means helping people and organisations become able to do a job well on their own and keep doing it over time.
simpleVsTechnical.technical: More technically, capacity-building is a deliberate intervention to strengthen individual competencies, organisational arrangements and enabling systems. Inputs such as funding, training, technical assistance and infrastructure are combined with process changes such as standard operating procedures, role definition, coordination mechanisms and monitoring. The aim is durable institutional capability: the ability to perform functions, manage risks, comply with mandates and adapt as conditions change. In AI governance, this can include regulatory skills, procurement literacy, data governance practices, assurance methods and cross-border cooperation. The term is broad, and in practice different organisations may emphasise different layers: human skills, organisational performance, institutional frameworks or all three.

keyTakeaway: The real test is not whether support was delivered, but whether people and institutions can now do the work reliably and keep improving.

quickCheck.question: Which example best fits capacity-building?
options: Holding one public lecture about AI trends
Buying software licences for staff without guidance or follow-up
Training staff, creating a review checklist and assigning a team to maintain the process
Hiring an external consultant to make all decisions indefinitely
quickCheck.explanation: Capacity-building combines skills, tools and organisational processes so capability lasts. The third option goes beyond awareness, purchases or dependence on outside experts.
